nameStory: The red-necked phalarope gets its name from the rusty-red patch that adorns the female's neck during breeding season. Like many bird names, it's a straightforward description of the most eye-catching feature that early naturalists noticed when they first classified this small shorebird.
description: The red-necked phalarope is a petite, delicate shorebird about the size of a sparrow that spends most of its life on the open ocean. These remarkable birds have an unusual lifestyle - they swim and spin in circles on the water's surface to stir up tiny floating creatures to eat. With their needle-thin bills and buoyant bodies, they look more like miniature gulls than typical sandpipers. They're quite small, measuring only about 7-8 inches long with a wingspan around 16 inches.

idTips.label: Swimming behavior
idTips.description: Watch for tiny birds spinning in tight circles on the water surface like living tops, creating small whirlpools to bring food up from below - no other New England shorebird does this

idTips.label: Bill shape
idTips.description: Thin, needle-like black bill that's much more delicate and straight than the thicker, slightly curved bills of most sandpipers

idTips.label: Body on water
idTips.description: Sits high and buoyant on water like a tiny cork, with a noticeably white belly that's easy to see from below when they're swimming

idTips.label: Breeding colors
idTips.description: Females in spring show a distinctive rusty-red neck patch and dark gray back with bright white stripes, while males are much duller

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Quick, erratic flight with rapid wingbeats, often calling with sharp 'kit' notes that sound like squeaky toys

idTips.label: Flock behavior
idTips.description: Often seen in small groups all spinning together on the water, creating a mesmerizing display of synchronized swimming

habitat: Red-necked phalaropes are most commonly seen in New England during migration on coastal waters, bays, and occasionally large inland lakes and ponds. They prefer areas where currents or wind create upwelling that brings tiny marine creatures to the surface. Unlike most shorebirds that probe in mud, these birds stick to open water areas where they can swim freely.

seasonality.spring: Most likely to be spotted in late April through May during northward migration, when females show their brightest rusty-red neck patches and bold plumage patterns.
seasonality.summer: Very rarely seen in summer as they breed far north in the Arctic tundra, though occasional stragglers might appear in coastal waters.
seasonality.fall: Best viewing season from August through September when both adults and young birds pass through in duller, grayer plumage that lacks the distinctive red coloring.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England as they spend winter far out at sea in tropical waters, making them true ocean nomads.

funFact: Red-necked phalaropes have completely reversed gender roles - the colorful females court the drab males, then abandon them to incubate the eggs and raise the chicks alone while the females head off to sea for the rest of the summer!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Red Phalaropes, but Red-necked Phalaropes have thinner, more needle-like bills (Red Phalaropes have thicker, slightly flattened bills). Memory trick: Red-necked = needle-thin, Red Phalarope = robust and thick. Wilson's Phalaropes are larger with longer, thinner necks and are rarely seen in coastal New England waters.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'phalarope' (meaning 'coot-footed' in Greek), these birds don't actually have lobed toes like coots do. The name is a bit of a misnomer from early taxonomists who grouped them incorrectly. They're also sometimes called 'northern phalaropes' or 'hyperborean phalaropes' in older field guides.
compareHints: Among the three phalarope species, Red-necked Phalaropes are the smallest and most needle-billed. Red Phalaropes are chunkier with thicker, more flattened bills and show more extensive red in breeding plumage. Wilson's Phalaropes are the largest, with the longest necks and bills, and prefer freshwater over saltwater habitats.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wilson's Phalarope is larger than the Red-necked and Red Phalaropes, with a longer, thinner bill and longer legs.
Red Phalarope is stockier than Red-necked Phalarope with a much thicker bill and more buoyant posture on water.
